body_markdown:
The Toyota Camry is a practical family sedan that offers excellent fuel economy thanks to a standard hybrid powertrain. The Honda Accord is also a practical family sedan, with just a bit more fun-to-drive flair than the Toyota. Rounding out the trio of practical family sedans from Japan is the Nissan Altima … which has the dubious honor of being a meme.


How did Nissan’s bread-and-butter mainstay become internet-famous? In the same way many people go viral online: through a series of poor decisions. While CEO Carlos Ghosn helped return Nissan to profitability in the early 2000s by aggressively cutting costs, that same approach spelled disaster for the company after the 2008 recession. As Honda and Toyota continued to retain Accord and Camry loyalists along with their quality standards, Nissan turned to fleet sales to chase Ghosn’s ambitious goal of 10% U.S. market share by 2017. The downside? When rental-fleet operators dump cars into the used market, those vehicles tend to go from one hard life to another. Used Altimas provided decent, inexpensive transportation, but all too often, their owners treated them with a total lack of mechanical sympathy.


During the 2010s, whenever a sedan with mismatched wheels whizzed past you at Mach 2, it was practically guaranteed to be an Altima, and thus the phrase Big Altima Energy emerged. (In 2020, its cultural importance was indicated by the establishment of a dedicated Facebook page, which, as of this writing, has 229,681 members and 8407 posts in the last month.) Possibly the peak of leaning into this joke happened in 2022, when someone shipped a rental-spec, four-cylinder Altima 2.5S to Germany and drove it around the Nürburgring.


Nissan


What at first seemed like pure mockery of the Altima’s so-so reputation morphed into a sort of grudging admiration. Ask any car enthusiast, and they’ll tell you that in the same way the fastest car in the world is a rental car, hammering on a beat-up Altima is a lot more fun than barely driving a sports car to preserve its resale value.


Aside from being an inside joke on the internet, the current Altima is a bit of an also-ran in the mainstream sedan market. Nissan might as well call it the Alternativema, as it’s inexpensive but doesn’t really outshine its rivals.


Still, cash-strapped Nissan seems determined to keep the sedan around, even as rumors of its impending cancellation swirl. If the Altima nameplate does fall victim to the rise of the crossover, will anyone preserve these cars? Well, there is one model possibly worth saving: the 2005–06 Nissan Altima SE-R.


Nissan


## The Poor Man’s BMW


The idea that a Nissan could be a collector car might have been scoffed at a couple of decades ago, but once the Skyline GT-R became a six-figure car, people stopped laughing. That said, when it comes to cars that were sold in the U.S. market, the standouts aren’t quite as striking as “Godzilla” was in the Japanese market.


The first models to see values rise weren’t badged as Nissans at all, but as Datsuns. The 510 and the 240Z were the first Datsuns (or Nissans) to be added to the Hagerty Price Guide, and both are now sought-after cars. Though it’s difficult to find today, back in the late ’60s and early ’70s[the plucky little 510](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/remembrance-day-and-a-datsun-510/) earned fans with its combination of BMW 2002-ish performance and a significantly lower price.


Winding the clock forward, we can find the 510’s spiritual ancestor in the third-generation Sentra, which launched in 1990. The standard versions of these little sedans were more functional than fun, but Nissan did push the boat out with a special model, the Sentra SE-R.


Nissan


On the surface, the B13-chassis Sentra SE-R was not particularly exciting to look at—just a box on a box with the edges sanded off. But under the hood was a 2.0-liter inline-four with double overhead camshafts, producing a punchy 140 horsepower. With under 2600 pounds to move, disc brakes, and fully independent suspension at all corners, this Sentra was a little pocket rocket.


Again, the BMW comparison reared its head. The Sentra SE-R did have compact economy roots and the wrong set of driven wheels, but it was quicker than a contemporary 318i for one half the price. Nissan’s original SE-R model wasn’t a volume seller like hotter Honda Civic variants, but it became one of those if-you-know-you-know cars.


While Sentra SE-Rs did offer more zip than the mainstream offerings, they weren’t terribly exciting. However, when it came to the Altima, the SE-R badge meant something special.


## A 350Z for Mom and Dad


Nissan


The story of the Altima 3.5 SE that debuted for the 2002 model year is strikingly similar to that of[the Taurus SHO](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/ford-taurus-sho-history/) , created when Ford dropped a Yamaha-tuned V-6 into a volume-selling sedan in 1989. It found an eager market among people with BMW dreams and Budweiser budgets.


The Altima 3.5 SE asked the question, “Are you interested in doing the school run and then some burnouts?” The answer was a resounding, “Yes, please.” In the showroom, the Altima pinched a little of the Maxima’s aura, but the latter’s V-6 had a slight power advantage, and the 3.5 SE helped the 240-hp Altima genuinely differentiate itself from the Accord and the Camry. The Toyota was smooth and a bit boring. The Accord was the handler. The V-6 Altima brought the muscle.


So successfully did the Altima hit the market that, for 2005, Nissan decided to grace its V-6 sedan with the SE-R moniker. With the contemporary 350Z coupe and roadster sitting right next to it in showrooms, it was only natural to lean more into the Altima’s sporting character.


Nissan


Nissan


Nissan


The SE-R was everything the Altima 3.5 SE offered, just one click extra. Output rose to 260 hp, mostly thanks to a freer-flowing exhaust. The manual transmission got an extra gear, with a total of six forward speeds (a five-speed automatic was still an available option). The suspension was tuned to be much stiffer, and a set of decidedly handsome forged 18-inch alloy wheels were fitted. Behind these lurked the larger Brembo brakes from the Maxima.


Nissan


Nissan


Inside, the SE-R got as much standard equipment as Nissan could pack in. It boasted an eight-speaker Bose stereo and six-disc CD changer, plus well-bolstered seats that suited the car’s purposeful personality. The three-pod gauge cluster on the dash included oil pressure (handy), instant-read fuel consumption (not that handy), and battery voltage (basically useless information). However, if the point was a car that looked a bit Z-adjacent while offering the practicality of a four-door, mission accomplished.


Nissan


The Altima was a bit rowdy to drive, with slightly too much power for the chassis and without a proper limited-slip differential. The suspension was also quite stiff, and getting that 260 hp to the road required patience on the throttle.


However, it was precisely that lack of refinement that made the SE-R an absolute hoot. It was nowhere near as polished as a contemporary 5 Series, but it wasn’t trying to be. Put it this way: People expect the *Reacher* TV series to have *some* kind of plot, but they’re mostly showing up to watch a large man (Alan Ritchson) punch things. The Altima SE-R is basically an Alan Ritchson 3.5 SE.


Nissan


Since the SE-R was sold only for two years and wasn’t likely to be as pampered as a same-year 350Z, finding a clean example of the Maximum-Altima Altima is a bit tricky. The six-speed is the option to hunt down, in our view—not only is it more engaging than the automatic, but with any luck, a manual-transmission Altima SE-R may also have enjoyed slightly more mechanically sympathetic owners.


Two decades after it left the market, the Altima SE-R makes the case that there is at least one piece of Altima history worth preserving. It was the only Nissan that was just as rowdy as the drivers who contributed to the Altima’s rather infamous reputation.
